methods.name: RotMoLE
methods.full_name: RotMoLE: Rotatable Mixture of Low-rank Experts (MoE-LoRA with a rotation gate)
methods.paper_title: RotMoLE: Enhancing Mixture of Low-Rank Experts through Rotational Gating Mechanism
methods.formula_latex: h=W_0x+\sum_{i\in\mathrm{TopK}(g(x))}g_i(x)\,B_i\,R_i(x)\,A_i\,x,\quad g(x)=\mathrm{softmax}(W_gx),\ \ \theta(x)=2\pi\,\sigma(W_\theta x)-\pi\in(-\pi,\pi)^{n};\ \ r=2:\ R_i=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta_i&-\sin\theta_i\\ \sin\theta_i&\cos\theta_i\end{pmatrix};\ \ r>2:\ e_{1,i}=\frac{A_ix}{\|A_ix\|},\ e_{2,i}=\frac{q_i-(q_i^{\top}e_{1,i})e_{1,i}}{\|q_i-(q_i^{\top}e_{1,i})e_{1,i}\|},\ R_i=[e_{1,i}\ e_{2,i}]\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta_i&-\sin\theta_i\\ \sin\theta_i&\cos\theta_i\end{pmatrix}[e_{1,i}\ e_{2,i}]^{\top},\ \text{so } R_iA_ix=\cos\theta_i\,A_ix+\sin\theta_i\,\|A_ix\|\,e_{2,i};\ \ B_i\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r},\ A_i\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}},\ W_g,W_\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{in}},\ q_i\in\mathbb{R}^{r};\ \text{frozen: } W_0;\ \text{trained: } \{A_i,B_i,q_i\}_{i=1}^{n},\ W_g,\ W_\theta
methods.trainable_params: n\,r(d_{in}+d_{out})+2n\,d_{in}+n\,r\ \text{per adapted matrix } (n \text{ experts, scaling gate } W_g,\ \text{rotation gate } W_\theta,\ \text{centres } q_i;\ \text{the } nr \text{ term is absent when } r=2);\ \text{overhead over a plain MoE-LoRA: } n\,d_{in}\,(+\,n\,r)
methods.locus: q_proj, k_proj, v_proj and o_proj of only the first quarter of the layers (layers 0-6 of Llama-3.2-3B, 0-8 of Qwen-2.5-3B, 0-9 of GLM-4-9B); experiments use r in {2, 3, 4, 6}, n in {2, 3, 4, 5} experts and top-k with k in {2, 3}
methods.structure: Per-token mixture of \(n\) LoRA experts in which the router returns, for each selected expert, a scale \(g_i(x)\) and a rotation \(R_i(x)\in SO(r)\) that acts in that expert's rank space, between \(A_i\) and \(B_i\). For \(r>2\) the rotation is a single planar (Givens-type) rotation by \(\theta_i(x)\) in \(\mathrm{span}(A_ix,q_i)\). It turns the code \(A_ix\) towards or away from a learned per-expert centre \(q_i\) and preserves \(\|A_ix\|\). The printed \(R_i\) is the rank-2 block \([e_1\,e_2]\,\mathrm{Rot}(\theta_i)\,[e_1\,e_2]^{\top}\). Because \(A_ix\) lies in that plane, it acts on \(A_ix\) exactly like the full rotation \(I_r+(\cos\theta_i-1)(e_1e_1^{\top}+e_2e_2^{\top})+\sin\theta_i(e_2e_1^{\top}-e_1e_2^{\top})\). Gauge reading (derived here): a constant \(R\) placed between \(B\) and \(A\) would be absorbed by the LoRA gauge, \((B,A)\mapsto(BR,A)\), and add nothing. RotMoLE's \(R_i\) depends on \(x\), both through \(\theta_i(x)\) and through the plane, which contains \(A_ix\). The expert map \(x\mapsto B_iR_i(x)A_ix\) is therefore a nonlinear, norm-preserving reshaping of each expert's code, and it enlarges the function class. The construction uses the Euclidean norm and Gram-Schmidt on rank space. Each expert is therefore invariant under \((B_i,A_i,q_i)\mapsto(B_iO,O^{\top}A_i,O^{\top}q_i)\) for \(O\in O(r)\), with \(R_i\mapsto O^{\top}R_iO\), but not under a general \(G\in GL(r)\): the residual gauge group of each expert drops from \(GL(r)\) to \(O(r)\). For \(r=2\) the fixed-basis rotation is equivariant under \(SO(2)\); a reflection additionally needs \(W_\theta\mapsto-W_\theta\). Top-\(k\) selection uses only \(g\). The paper does not treat the degenerate case \(q_i\parallel A_ix\).
methods.mergeable_reason: The scales \(g_i(x)\), the angles \(\theta_i(x)\) and the plane \(\mathrm{span}(A_ix,q_i)\) all depend on the token. \(\sum_i g_iB_iR_i(x)A_i\) is therefore not a fixed matrix and cannot be folded into \(W_0\).
methods.identity_at_init: Yes. \(B_i=0\) (LoRA convention) gives \(\Delta W x=0\). \(W_\theta=0\) gives \(\theta_i=0\), so \(R_iA_ix=A_ix\) and the model starts as a conventional MoE-LoRA. The centres \(q_i\) are Kaiming-uniform initialised.
methods.key_idea: A scalar gate can only rescale an expert's output along a fixed direction. LoRA experts have an \(r\)-dimensional bottleneck, so an input-dependent rotation of the code \(A_ix\) costs only \(n\,d_{in}+n\,r\) extra parameters. Each selected expert can then also be turned, which lets a few shared experts serve several tasks differently.
methods.results_note: On a jointly trained CSQA/OBQA/SIQA mixture with Qwen-2.5-3B (r=6, n=4, k=2), RotMoLE averages 45.82% accuracy, against 41.42 for AdaMoLE, 35.66 for MoLA and 34.57 for MoCLE. Against the plain MoE-LoRA baseline it is better in 7 of 8 QA configurations.

relations.note: Cited as the canonical MoE-LoRA, h = W_0x + sum_i g_i B_iA_ix with a scalar softmax gate. RotMoLE adds a rotation gate inside each expert's rank space.
Cited (Li et al., 2024) as the top-k MoE-LoRA form. RotMoLE keeps top-k selection on the scalar gate values and adds per-expert rotations.

Both put an r x r map between B and A. MoSLoRA's mixer is input-independent, so it stays within the gauge reach and does not change LoRA's function class. RotMoLE's rotation is token-dependent and does change it. MoSLoRA is not cited.
Another way to diversify LoRA experts under a router: HydraLoRA shares A and routes over several B heads, while RotMoLE keeps full experts and rotates their codes. HydraLoRA is not cited.

methods.trainable_params: r(d_{in}+d_{out})\ \text{per adapted matrix, as in LoRA, with AdamW moments for the factors only. The base matrix is rewritten at every re-split, so the deliverable is the dense merged } W_T \text{, not a detachable adapter}
methods.locus: LoRA target matrices of DeBERTaV3-base (GLUE, r=4, setup of AdaLoRA), LLaMA2-7B and LLaMA3-8B (commonsense reasoning, r=8, setup of Lion et al. 2025) and Gemma-3-12B (MetaMathQA)
methods.structure: Rebasing inside a single LoRA run. Before each step the current product is re-split as \(W_t=\tilde W_0^{(t)}+\tilde B_t\tilde A_t\) with column- and row-scaled factors. The difference \(B_t\,\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf 1-\alpha_t\circ\beta_t)\,A_t\) is merged into the frozen weight. The summed increments therefore no longer telescope to \(B_TA_T\), and \(W_T-W_0\) can reach high rank: average rank 54 at \(r=4\) on RTE, and thousands of singular values above 0.005 at \(r=8\) on LLaMA2-7B. Gauge reading (derived here): where \(\alpha\circ\beta>0\), write \(\alpha=c\circ s\) and \(\beta=c^{-1}\circ s\) elementwise. The move is then a diagonal (maximal-torus) gauge transformation \((B,A)\mapsto(B\,\mathrm{diag}(c),\mathrm{diag}(c)^{-1}A)\), which leaves \(W\) fixed but changes the next step because LoRA's gradient descent is not gauge-invariant. It is followed by a per-direction rescaling \(\mathrm{diag}(s^{\circ2})\) of the adapter, whose complement is merged. Only diagonal scalings are used, because they are the transformations under which Adam's moment estimates transform in closed form (Lemmas 3.3 and 3.6); a full-matrix or row-wise transform is intractable. The unrestricted optimum of the same surrogate (Theorem 3.2) takes \(\tilde B\) and \(\tilde A^{\top}\) from \(2r\) top singular vectors of \(G_t\), split into two sets of \(r\), each up to an \(O(r)\) factor. LoRA-GA's initialisation is the \(t=0\), identity-rotation case. In the paper's printed Theorem 3.7, the second block matrix lists \(\mathbf B_t\) before \(\mathbf A_t^{\top}\nabla\ell\) and needs a transpose. The pairing given in formula_latex, \(S_{in}=[G^{\top}B,\ A^{\top}]\), is the one consistent with the stated \(\lambda\) and objective (re-derived here). The paper's 'fixed subspace' remark is the telescoping identity \(\sum_t\Delta W_t=B_TA_T\), i.e. a rank-\(r\) bound on vanilla LoRA's cumulative update.
methods.mergeable_reason: The adapter is merged into the base at every re-split and the final model is the dense \(W_T\). Because \(W_0^{(t)}\) itself changes, \(W_T-W_0\) is high-rank and cannot be shipped as a rank-\(r\) adapter; the paper stores the full merged matrix.
methods.identity_at_init: Yes. Standard LoRA initialisation has one zero factor; the paper puts the Gaussian on the \(d_{out}\times r\) factor and zeros on the \(d_{in}\) side. This gives \(W_0^{(0)}+B_0A_0=W_0\), and every later re-split preserves \(W_t\) exactly.
methods.key_idea: Vanilla LoRA's increments telescope, \(\sum_t\Delta W_t=B_TA_T\), so the cumulative update never exceeds rank \(r\). ScaLoRA merges and re-factors at every step and rescales Adam's moments to match, so it accumulates a high-rank update with no restarts. The column scaling of the current factors is chosen in closed form to minimise a smoothness upper bound on the next loss, which is the same as best matching the full fine-tuning step \(-G_t/L\).
methods.results_note: With r=8, ScaLoRA-I averages 74.75 on eight commonsense tasks with LLaMA2-7B and ScaLoRA averages 77.85 with LLaMA3-8B. Both are above LoRA (73.63/76.83), ReLoRA, LoRA-GA, MoRA and HiRA, and level with or above rank-32 LoRA (74.52/77.54), at about 0.01 GB of extra memory over LoRA.

relations.note: Baseline. ReLoRA also merges low-rank increments into the base, but only rarely, with re-initialised factors, reset optimizer state and LR re-warm-up. ScaLoRA re-splits at every step, keeps scaled factors and transforms their moments.
The paper states that LoRA-GA's gradient-SVD initialisation is the t=0, identity-rotation case of Theorem 3.2's optimal-adapter condition. LoRA-GA is also a commonsense baseline.
High-rank baseline. The paper reports that HiRA's Hadamard update has high Euclidean rank but intrinsic rank r, and needs O(d_out d_in) extra memory, against ScaLoRA's O((d_out + d_in + r) r).
High-rank baseline (square-matrix compress/decompress); about 1 GB of extra memory on LLaMA3-8B.
Another rebasing scheme: tune a LoRA, merge it, start a new one and reset optimizer state. ScaLoRA avoids such restarts. COLA is not cited.
Also feeds low-rank increments into the base weight without restarts, but by adding the product's per-step change rather than by an optimal re-split. Delta-LoRA is not cited.

methods.name: LoRA-S (AdamS, LRACS)
methods.full_name: LoRA-S: Sylvester-equation horizontal-lift scheme for LoRA optimizers (Adam-Sylvester and LRACS)
methods.paper_title: LoRA-S: An Efficient Low Rank Adaptation scheme via Sylvester equation
methods.formula_latex: W=W_0+BA,\ B\in\mathbb{R}_*^{d_{out}\times r},\ A\in\mathbb{R}_*^{r\times d_{in}}\ (\text{paper: } M=B,\ N=A^{\top},\ X=MN^{\top});\ G_t=\nabla_W\mathcal L;\ \text{matrix-space direction } \dot X_t=-\eta\,\tilde X_t:\ \text{AdamS: } m_t=\beta_1m_{t-1}+(1-\beta_1)G_t,\ v_t=\beta_2v_{t-1}+(1-\beta_2)G_t^{\odot2},\ \tilde X_t=m_t/\sqrt{v_t};\ \text{LRACS: } \tilde X_t=\mathrm{Diag}(m_q^{t})^{-1/2}\,G_t\,\mathrm{Diag}(m_s^{t})^{-1/2}\ (\text{row and column statistics, as in RACS});\ \text{Sylvester: } (B^{\top}B)(AA^{\top})K_t+K_t(B^{\top}B)(AA^{\top})=B^{\top}\dot X_tA^{\top};\ \text{lift: } \dot B=(\dot X_tA^{\top}-BAA^{\top}K_t)(AA^{\top})^{-1},\ \ \dot A=(B^{\top}B)^{-1}(B^{\top}\dot X_t-K_tB^{\top}BA);\ \ (B,A)\leftarrow(B+\dot B,\ A+\dot A);\ \text{frozen: } W_0;\ \text{trained: } B,A\ (\text{no weight decay})
methods.trainable_params: r(d_{in}+d_{out})\ \text{per adapted matrix (plain LoRA factors). Optimizer state: } O(d_{out}d_{in}) \text{ matrix-space Adam moments for AdamS (the poster mentions a low-memory variant) and } O(d_{out}+d_{in}+1) \text{ for LRACS}
methods.locus: LoRA-adapted weights of transformer models. The poster reports Mix-of-Show image customisation with Stable Diffusion LoRAs (r = 4, 8, 16) and GPT-2 medium on E2E NLG (r = 4).
methods.structure: Optimizer for plain LoRA factors, built on the quotient \((\mathbb R_*^{d_{out}\times r}\times\mathbb R_*^{r\times d_{in}})/GL(r)\cong\mathcal M_r\). The base optimizer (Adam or RACS) preconditions the full-matrix gradient in matrix space. An \(r\times r\) Sylvester equation and a horizontal lift then map the resulting direction \(\dot X\) to factor updates. Derived here from the poster's formulas: \(\dot BA+B\dot A=P_B\dot X+\dot XP_A-P_B\dot XP_A\), with \(P_B=B(B^{\top}B)^{-1}B^{\top}\) and \(P_A=A^{\top}(AA^{\top})^{-1}A\). So the first-order change of \(W\) is the orthogonal projection of \(\dot X\) onto the tangent space \(T_{BA}\mathcal M_r\). The Sylvester matrix \(K\) is exactly what removes the double-counted term \(P_B\dot XP_A\), which the \(K=0\) lift contains; that lift is scaled GD, i.e. Riemannian-preconditioned LoRA. Setting \(K=\epsilon I\) instead turns the \(K\) terms into \(-\epsilon B\) and \(-\epsilon A\), i.e. decoupled weight decay on both factors. This is the paper's reading of weight decay as a crude approximation of \(K\), and the reason it removes the decay hyperparameter. The update is equivariant under \((B,A)\mapsto(BR,R^{-1}A)\), with \(K\mapsto R^{\top}KR^{-\top}\), so the induced \(W\) update depends only on \(BA\). This is the poster's Theorem 1: transformation invariance plus the paper's 'efficient feature learning' condition. Each step costs \(\Omega(d_{out}d_{in}r)+O(r^{3}+(d_{out}+d_{in})r^{2})\).
methods.mergeable_reason: Only the optimizer changes. The trained adapter is a standard \(BA\) that folds into \(W_0\).
methods.identity_at_init: Not specified in the material available. The lift needs \((AA^{\top})^{-1}\) and \((B^{\top}B)^{-1}\), i.e. full-rank factors in \(\mathbb R_*\), so LoRA's usual \(B=0\) start lies outside its domain. The paper must use a nonzero or damped start, which the poster does not show.
methods.key_idea: Precondition in matrix space, then lift. Any matrix-space optimizer becomes a gauge-invariant LoRA optimizer once its direction is lifted to the factors through the quotient geometry, with an \(r\times r\) Sylvester solve fixing the correction term. The \(\epsilon I\) weight-decay term of factor optimizers is reinterpreted as a crude approximation of that Sylvester matrix and dropped.
methods.results_note: According to the official ICLR poster, with rank-4 LoRA on GPT-2 medium (E2E NLG) LRACS reaches BLEU 70.4, against 69.3 for LoRA-RITE and 68.6 for AdamW. On Mix-of-Show image customisation, AdamS at rank 16 reaches CLIP 32.64 / FID 46.32, against 31.90 / 55.68 for LoRA-RITE.

relations.note: With K=0 and Xdot=-eta G, the lift is exactly the scaled-GD step Bdot = -eta G A^T (A A^T)^{-1}, Adot = -eta (B^T B)^{-1} B^T G of Riemannian-preconditioned LoRA, which appears as the 'Scaled GD' baseline on the poster. LoRA-S adds the Sylvester correction and allows arbitrary matrix-space preconditioners (derived here).
Main transformation-invariant baseline. LoRA-RITE preconditions in orthonormal factor bases; LoRA-S preconditions in matrix space and then lifts.

Citation not checked (full paper unavailable). LoRA-Pro's equivalent gradient is also the tangent-space projection P_B G + G P_A - P_B G P_A, and it fixes its free r x r matrix with a Sylvester equation. LoRA-S applies the same projection to a preconditioned matrix-space direction (derived here).

Provides the quotient manifold (R_*^{m x r} x R_*^{n x r})/GL(r) and the horizontal-lift machinery that LoRA-S instantiates for LoRA. The citation could not be checked because the paper PDF was unavailable.

methods.name: DiaBlo
methods.full_name: DiaBlo: fine-tuning only the diagonal blocks of weight matrices
methods.paper_title: DiaBlo: Diagonal Blocks Are Sufficient For Finetuning
methods.formula_latex: h=(W_0+D)\,x,\quad D=\mathrm{blockdiag}(D_1,\dots,D_N)=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{N}D_i,\ \ D_i\in\mathbb{R}^{\frac{d_{out}}{N}\times\frac{d_{in}}{N}};\ \ (Dx)_i=D_ix_i\ (\text{one batched matmul over the } N \text{ input and output slices});\ \ \nabla_{D_i}\mathcal L=\big(\nabla_W\mathcal L\big)_{ii};\ \ D=0 \text{ at init};\ \text{frozen: } W_0 \text{ (in particular every off-diagonal block)};\ \text{trained: } D_1,\dots,D_N
methods.trainable_params: \frac{d_{in}d_{out}}{N}\ \text{per adapted matrix (typically } N\in\{32,64,128\}\text{; } N=64 \text{ is about 1.04\% of Llama2-7B with } q,k,v,\mathrm{up},\mathrm{down}\text{ adapted)}
methods.locus: Linear projections of the LLM: q, k, v, up and down (FP16 commonsense and math runs), or q, k, v, o, gate, up and down (BF16, code, safety and quantized runs), on Llama2-7B/13B, Llama3-8B, Llama-13B and Mistral-7B; all linear layers except embeddings and the LM head for T5-base
methods.structure: A fixed block-diagonal sparsity pattern on \(\Delta W\): \(N\) independent dense blocks on the diagonal. Block \(i\) maps the \(i\)-th slice of \(d_{in}/N\) input coordinates to the \(i\)-th slice of \(d_{out}/N\) output coordinates, so \(\mathrm{rank}(\Delta W)\) can reach \(\min(d_{in},d_{out})\) with \(d_{in}d_{out}/N\) parameters. The update set is a linear subspace, not a product manifold. There is therefore no \(GL(r)\) gauge, the loss restricted to it is the original loss (convex in \(D\) whenever it is convex in \(W\)), and AdamW on \(D\) is AdamW on the masked entries of \(W\). The block structure is tied to the coordinate basis of the hidden units: it is not invariant to permuting or rotating them. Relative to neighbouring shapes, factoring each block at rank \(r/N\) gives MELoRA, a full \(N\times N\) grid of low-rank blocks gives GraLoRA, and choosing the blocks by gradient magnitude gives SMT. Linear least squares (Theorem 1): if the inputs \(X\) are generic of rank \(r\) and \(N\le d_{in}/r\), every DiaBlo minimiser is a full fine-tuning minimiser. This uses \(d_{in}d_{out}/N\ge d_{out}r\) parameters, against LoRA's \((d_{in}+d_{out})r\). Nonlinear case (Theorem 2): if \(X\) and \(g_Y\) are generic of ranks \(r_1\) and \(r_2\) and \(N\ge\lceil r_1N/d_{in}\rceil\lceil r_2N/d_{out}\rceil\), DiaBlo's stationary points are stationary for full fine-tuning. Sizes that \(N\) does not divide use blocks of \(\lceil d/N\rceil\) with zero padding.
methods.mergeable_reason: \(D\) is a \(d_{out}\times d_{in}\) block-diagonal matrix added to \(W_0\). It can be folded in, or stored compactly as an \(N\times\frac{d_{out}}{N}\times\frac{d_{in}}{N}\) tensor. On a quantized base (the GPTQ-DiaBlo and MagR-DiaBlo runs), merging needs re-quantization.
methods.identity_at_init: Yes. \(D=0\), and since there is no product the gradient \(\nabla_{D_i}\mathcal L=(\nabla_W\mathcal L)_{ii}\) is nonzero from the first step. There is no LoRA-style zero-factor stall and no special initialisation.
methods.key_idea: Update a structured subset of the weights directly instead of a low-rank product. Training only the diagonal blocks keeps LoRA-like memory and speed, since the forward pass is one batched matmul. It removes the bilinear factorisation's sensitivity to initialisation and optimizer. Under low-rank activations and gradients it provably reaches full fine-tuning minimisers in the linear case, and full fine-tuning stationary points in general.
methods.results_note: On commonsense reasoning DiaBlo reaches an 87.3 average with Llama3-8B (N=64, 1.04% of parameters), against 85.2 for DoRA r=32 and 80.8 for LoRA r=32. On MetaMathQA with Llama2-7B (N=32, 2.09%) it averages 43.4 on GSM8K/MATH, against 43.2 for full fine-tuning.

relations.note: MELoRA factors each diagonal block as B_iA_i of rank r/N, while DiaBlo trains the same blocks at full block rank. For equal N, MELoRA's update set is a subset of DiaBlo's. MELoRA is not cited.

Cited baseline. SMT selects the sub-matrices with the largest warm-up gradients; DiaBlo fixes the pattern to the diagonal blocks. DiaBlo beats SMT on commonsense reasoning with fewer parameters (83.5 vs 81.8 on Llama2-7B).
GraLoRA tiles the full N x N block grid with low-rank adapters; DiaBlo keeps only the diagonal tiles but makes them dense. GraLoRA is not cited.

Another structured, non-product shape: MiSS replicates one small trainable shard across the matrix (rank at most r), while DiaBlo gives each diagonal block its own dense parameters. MiSS is not cited.
Strongest LoRA-family baseline on commonsense reasoning. DiaBlo exceeds it on Llama2-7B, Llama3-8B and Llama-13B.

Quantized-base baseline. DiaBlo fine-tunes GPTQ/MagR-quantized Llama2 models with no joint quantization and initialisation procedure, and is reported to match or exceed LoftQ and ApiQ at 4 and 2 bits.

methods.name: QZO
methods.full_name: QZO: Quantized Zeroth-order Optimization (Q-SPSA with directional-derivative clipping)
methods.paper_title: Fine-tuning Quantized Neural Networks with Zeroth-order Optimization
methods.formula_latex: \hat W=\Delta\odot\overline W,\ \ \overline W\ \text{frozen low-bit codes (GPTQ int4 with group size } g=128\text{, or AQLM 2-bit codebooks)},\ \ \Delta=S\otimes\mathbf 1_{1\times g},\ S\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{d_{out}\times d_{in}/g}\ (\text{channel-wise } S\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}} \text{ for AQLM});\ \ d=\frac{\mathcal L((\Delta+\epsilon z)\odot\overline W;\mathcal B)-\mathcal L((\Delta-\epsilon z)\odot\overline W;\mathcal B)}{2\epsilon},\ z\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\ \text{on the scale entries, regenerated from a seed};\ \ d'=\mathrm{clip}(d,-C,C);\ \ S\leftarrow\max(S-\eta\,d'z,\ 0);\ \text{frozen: the integer codes};\ \text{trained: the quantization scales (in the AQLM runs, non-quantized parameters are also updated by plain SPSA)};\ \text{no backward pass and no optimizer state}
methods.trainable_params: \frac{d_{out}d_{in}}{g}\ \text{scales per quantized matrix } (g=128;\ 5.03\times10^{7}\ \text{for OPT-6.7B, about } 0.76\%);\ d_{out}\ \text{for channel-wise AQLM scales};\ \text{optimizer memory } O(1) \text{ (a seed and a scalar)}
methods.locus: Quantization scales of all quantized linear layers: GPTQ 4-bit OPT-6.7B, Llama-2-7B and Llama-3.1-8B; AQLM 2-bit Llama-2-13B (channel-wise scales plus the non-quantized parts); also Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large
methods.structure: PEQA-type parametrisation trained with MeZO-style SPSA. The parametrisation is a group-wise multiplicative rescaling of frozen integer codes, \(\hat W=(S\otimes\mathbf 1_{1\times g})\odot\overline W\); per channel it is the left diagonal action \(\hat W=\mathrm{diag}(s)\,\overline W\). The gradient estimate is a rank-one random projection \(zz^{\top}\nabla_S\mathcal L\) of the scale gradient, computed from two forward passes of the quantized model. Weights are never de-quantized or re-quantized, and activations are not stored. Directional-derivative clipping caps the scalar \(d\) at \(C\) (100 in the paper), and the projection \(\max(\cdot,0)\) keeps the scales non-negative. Every code stays fixed, so the reachable set is \(\{(S\otimes\mathbf 1)\odot\overline W\}\), of dimension \(d_{out}d_{in}/g\). The paper's Theorem 1 states that the clipped estimate is unbiased, but its proof treats the clipping event as independent of \(z\). In general a clipped SPSA estimate is biased; the variance reduction from \(d'^{2}\le d^{2}\) does hold.
methods.mergeable_reason: The trained parameters are the quantization scales themselves. The result is an ordinary GPTQ or AQLM model with the same codes and inference kernels.
methods.identity_at_init: No adapter is added. Training starts from the post-training-quantized model, whose GPTQ/AQLM scales approximate but do not equal \(W_0\).
methods.key_idea: Zeroth-order training removes gradients and optimizer states, and quantization shrinks the weights. The two meet in the continuous quantization scales, which SPSA can perturb and update while the discrete codes stay fixed. Clipping the directional derivative keeps the noisy estimate stable.
methods.results_note: On 4-bit GPTQ Llama-2-7B, QZO needs 5.0 GB, against 14.8 GB for 16-bit MeZO and 26.0 GB for 16-bit SGD fine-tuning, and beats MeZO on four of five tasks (for example SST-2 90.0 vs 83.5). On OPT-6.7B it trails MeZO on most tasks.

relations.note: Uses MeZO's seed-regenerated SPSA and ZO-SGD, applied to the quantization scales of a 4- or 2-bit model instead of 16-bit weights. MeZO is the main baseline.
Trains the same object as PEQA, group-wise quantization scales over frozen integer codes, but without backpropagation, by combining it with MeZO-style estimation. PEQA is not cited.

Appendix comparison on OPT-6.7B: first-order QLoRA (5.6 GB) is more accurate than QZO (4.8 GB). A two-phase QZO+QLoRA variant (zeroth-order LoRA training, then QZO on the remaining scales) closes part of the gap at 4.9 GB.

Both are zeroth-order fine-tuning methods; AGZO is not cited. AGZO reduces estimator variance by perturbing 16-bit weights only along activation subspaces; QZO perturbs quantization scales and clips the directional derivative.

methods.name: PERK
methods.full_name: PERK: Parameter Efficient Reasoning over Knowledge (meta-learned test-time LoRA memory)
methods.paper_title: PERK: Long-Context Reasoning as Parameter-Efficient Test-Time Learning
methods.formula_latex: \phi^{(0)}=\theta_{\mathrm{adapter}}=\{(B_l,A_l)\},\ \ \phi^{(n+1)}=\mathrm{AdamW}_{\alpha_{l,n}}\big(\phi^{(n)},\ \nabla_{\phi}\mathcal L^{\psi}_{\mathrm{NLL}}(\phi^{(n)};\mathcal K)\big),\ n=0,\dots,N-1\ (N=4),\ \ \mathcal L^{\psi}_{\mathrm{NLL}}(\phi;\mathcal K)=-\sum_{c\in\mathrm{chunks}(\mathcal K)}\sum_{t}w_\psi(c_{\le t})\log p_{W_0,\phi}(c_t\mid c_{<t})\ (\approx256\text{-token chunks processed as one batch});\ \ \text{answer } q \text{ with } h=(W_0+B^{(N)}A^{(N)})x\ \text{and no context in the prompt};\ \ \min_{\theta_{\mathrm{adapter}},\{\alpha_{l,n}\},\psi}\ \mathbb{E}_{(\mathcal K,q,y)}\,\mathcal L_{\mathrm{reason}}\big(W_0,\phi^{(N)}(\theta_{\mathrm{adapter}},\mathcal K);q,y\big),\ \ \nabla_{\theta_{\mathrm{adapter}}}\mathcal L_{\mathrm{reason}}\approx\frac{\partial\mathcal L_{\mathrm{reason}}}{\partial\phi^{(N)}}\prod_{n=N-T}^{N-1}J^{(n)},\ J^{(n)}=I-\alpha H^{(n)}\ (\text{truncated unrolling, } T\in\{1,2\});\ \text{frozen: } W_0;\ \text{meta-trained: the LoRA initialisation, per-layer-per-step inner learning rates, token-weighting MLP } \psi;\ \text{test-time trained: the LoRA, once per context}
methods.trainable_params: r(d_{in}+d_{out})\ \text{per adapted matrix with } r=256\ (\text{rsLoRA}),\ \text{on all linear modules of every layer for models up to 1B and of the top 4 layers for 7B/8B models};\ \text{plus } L\times N \text{ meta-learned inner learning rates and a two-layer MLP token weighter. The same adapter is re-trained for every new context}
methods.locus: All linear modules (attention and MLP): every layer of GPT-2, Qwen-2.5-0.5B and LLaMA-3.2-1B; only the top 4 layers of Qwen-2.5-7B and LLaMA-3.1-8B
methods.structure: Bi-level, MAML-style meta-learning over a LoRA. The inner loop is test-time training of \(\Delta W=BA\) by \(N=4\) differentiable AdamW steps on the token-weighted NLL of the context. The context is chunked into a parallel batch, which decouples its length from the native window; chunk order is kept only through 'Document i:' tags in the text. The outer loop optimises the adapter's initial state \((B_0,A_0)\), the inner learning rates and the token-weighting network, so that the post-adaptation model answers questions without seeing the context. Meta-gradients are truncated to the last \(T\in\{1,2\}\) inner steps, so meta-training on 8K-token contexts fits on one GPU. The LoRA serves as a fast-weight memory: the context is written into parameters by gradient descent, not by a hypernetwork forward pass. Gauge remark (derived here): the inner loop is plain adaptive gradient descent on the factors, which is not invariant under \((B,A)\mapsto(BR,R^{-1}A)\). The outer loop therefore selects a particular representative of the initial adapter's orbit, and its conditioning decides what four inner steps can write. The learned object is that representative, not just the product \(B_0A_0\).
methods.mergeable_reason: After adaptation \(B^{(N)}A^{(N)}\) is an ordinary low-rank delta and could be folded into \(W_0\). It is specific to one context, however, and is regenerated by test-time training for each new one, so it is kept as a swappable module.
methods.identity_at_init: Not identity by design. Inference starts from the meta-learned adapter \(\theta_{\mathrm{adapter}}\), which is generally nonzero, so the model differs from the base even before test-time training. The base weights stay frozen, so dropping the adapter recovers the base model. The LoRA initialisation at the start of meta-training is not stated beyond 'default' PEFT settings.
methods.key_idea: Treat a LoRA as a fast-weight memory written by a few gradient steps on the context at test time. Meta-learn the adapter's starting point, step sizes and token weights, MAML-style with truncated unrolling to fit 8K-token contexts, so that the written adapter supports reasoning over long inputs rather than in-context retrieval.
methods.results_note: Trained on 8K-token contexts, PERK beats standard long-context fine-tuning (FT-ICR) on HotpotQA/TriviaQA by about 20 absolute points at the 0.5B scale and 15 at 7B. On BabiLong it leads by 23 points on average when extrapolating to 32K tokens.

relations.note: Same goal of internalising a context into a LoRA. Doc-to-LoRA amortises the write into one hypernetwork forward pass trained by context distillation; PERK writes it with meta-learned gradient steps at test time. D2L appeared later and is not cited.
SHINE is a single-pass in-context hypernetwork from context to LoRA; PERK is the gradient-based, test-time-training counterpart. SHINE is not cited.
Also maps a context to a parameter delta, but with a forward-pass generator instead of inner-loop optimisation. Not cited.
Cartridges compresses a corpus offline into a trained KV cache by self-study distillation, once per corpus. PERK trains a LoRA per context in four meta-learned steps. Not cited.
Uses rank-stabilised scaling for its rank-256 adapters.

notes: All six requested methods exist, all six are PEFT methods, and none duplicates a catalogued id; ids and arXiv numbers were checked against existing_index.json, which has no entry for any of them. Methods were read from their arXiv HTML method sections, except LoRA-S. Venues were verified as follows. RotMoLE is a NeurIPS 2026 poster in the official neurips.cc orals-posters JSON (OpenReview uGtHLqoW8K). ScaLoRA is in the ICML 2026 JSON ('Accept (regular)', OpenReview Skxb4UgTWU) and its arXiv comment says 'Accepted to ICML 2026'. LoRA-S (Guo2XGgxZA), DiaBlo (cZaI6GmjBm), PERK (qxDTe8fIyA) and QZO (mGeeRFToaW) are all 'Accept (Poster)' in the ICLR 2026 JSON. LoRA-S has no arXiv version, and OpenReview (forum, PDF and API) answered every request with a bot-verification challenge, which was not bypassed. Its formula was therefore transcribed from the official ICLR poster image (iclr.cc/media/PosterPDFs/ICLR 2026/10010449.png), which shows the Sylvester equation, the lift and the AdamS/LRACS updates, together with the ICLR abstract. Confidence for LoRA-S is medium. From those poster formulas I derived three things: the lift's first-order W update is the tangent-space projection of the matrix-space direction; K = eps*I reproduces decoupled weight decay; and the update is equivariant with K -> R^T K R^{-T}. These are marked 'derived here'. LoRA-S's year is 2025 because the ICLR 2026 submission was public on OpenReview in autumn 2025; the exact open date could not be read through the challenge. An empty GitHub repository, CleverWing/lora_s, describes itself as the official implementation and calls the paper an ICLR 2026 Spotlight, but the ICLR data says Poster. code_url is left empty. Year follows the first public version: ScaLoRA arXiv v1 2025-10-27, DiaBlo 2025-06-03, QZO 2025-05-19, PERK 2025-07-08, RotMoLE 2026-05-25. The PERK paper_title is the ICLR title; the arXiv title is 'PERK: Long-Context Reasoning as Test-Time Learning'. Corrections and caveats recorded in the entries: (i) ScaLoRA's 'fixed subspace' claim is the telescoping identity sum_t dW_t = B_T A_T, i.e. a rank-r bound. The printed Theorem 3.7 has a block-order/transpose typo in its second matrix; the pairing given in formula_latex was re-derived from the stated objective and lambda. (ii) QZO's Theorem 1 claims the clipped SPSA estimate is unbiased, but the proof ignores the dependence of the clipping event on z; only the variance bound holds in general. (iii) RotMoLE's printed R_i is a rank-2 planar block that acts as a full SO(r) rotation on A_i x. My gauge analysis finds that the rotation gate reduces each expert's residual gauge group from GL(r) to O(r), with q_i -> O^T q_i. None of the six is in Hugging Face PEFT (tuners directory and releases up to v0.21.2, 2026-10-01). Semantic Scholar was not queried. Not-yet-catalogued neighbours seen in these papers: AdaMoLE, MoLA, MoCLE and CoMoL (RotMoLE baselines and related work); QuZO (cited by QZO); RACS (the base optimizer lifted by LRACS); RECKONING and CaMeLS (PERK's predecessors for meta-learned knowledge encoding and token weighting). No standalone theory papers were added. The theorems of ScaLoRA (optimal low-rank step and scaling), DiaBlo (expressivity and stationarity) and LoRA-S (invariance) are recorded inside the method entries.
